- **Decimal fractions** [`decimal_fractions`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/decimal_fractions.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Astronomers, engineers and users of logarithm tables write decimals, in several notations. Money, weights and measures are not decimal, so merchants keep common fractions.
- **Negative numbers** [`negative_numbers`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/negative_numbers.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Algebraists calculate with them and bookkeepers think in debts, but textbooks still call negative roots 'false' and avoid them as answers.
- **Square roots and irrational numbers** [`square_roots_irrationals`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/square_roots_irrationals.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high
- **Logarithms** [`logarithms`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/logarithms.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Kepler adopted them for the Rudolphine Tables and Bürgi's own table was printed at Prague in 1620. Astronomers and a few engineers use Vlacq's tables; merchants and gunners do not. Local: Jesuit mathematicians; printed tables (Vlacq, Kepler) in college and court libraries.
- **Slide rule** [`slide_rule`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/slide_rule.md) — K1, use none, make medium, accept high. An English instrument, almost unknown in the German lands. Engineers here use the sector (proportional compass) instead. An instrument maker can engrave one from a log table. Local: instrument makers; fortress engineers and gunners as users. Elsewhere: England: Gunter's line, Oughtred's sliding rules, gaugers' rules.
- **Symbolic algebra** [`symbolic_algebra`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/symbolic_algebra.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Descartes's notation is the learned standard, though his books are on the Index. Jesuit teaching still leans on Clavius's older cossic style. Local: Jesuit professors of mathematics.
- **Solving quadratic and cubic equations** [`quadratic_cubic_equations`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/quadratic_cubic_equations.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high
- **Systems of linear equations (elimination and matrices)** [`linear_equations_matrices`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/linear_equations_matrices.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Small systems are solved by substitution or the rule of false position; there is no general elimination scheme and no notation for the array of coefficients.
- **Complex numbers** [`complex_numbers`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/complex_numbers.md) — K2, use none, make medium, accept low. Bombelli's rules are known to algebraists as a trick for the cubic; the quantities are called impossible or imaginary. No picture of them as points in a plane.
- **Prime numbers and number theory** [`prime_numbers_number_theory`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/prime_numbers_number_theory.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept low. Euclid's results are taught. Fermat's theorems circulated in letters without proofs (his works were printed in 1679) and are thought pretty but useless.
- **Combinatorics (permutations, combinations, Pascal's triangle)** [`combinatorics_permutations`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/combinatorics_permutations.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Counting combinations is fashionable through the Lullian art: Kircher's Ars magna sciendi is dedicated to Leopold I. Pascal's triangle treatise (1665) is rare here. Local: Kircher, Ars magna sciendi (1669). Elsewhere: Hanover: Leibniz, De arte combinatoria (1666).
- **Compound interest and exponential growth** [`compound_interest_exponential_growth`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/compound_interest_exponential_growth.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept medium. Court financiers and the Hofkammer reckon interest on war loans from printed tables. Nobody applies the same growth law to population or plague deaths. Local: Hofkammer. Elsewhere: Basel: Jakob Bernoulli studies continuous compounding (1683).
- **Deductive geometry and proof (Euclid, Pythagoras)** [`geometry_proof`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/geometry_proof.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Euclid in Clavius's edition is the core of Jesuit mathematics teaching; fortification is taught as applied geometry to young nobles. Local: Jesuit college and university; fortress engineers.
- **Pi and the measurement of the circle** [`pi_circle_measurement`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/pi_circle_measurement.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Craftsmen use 22/7, mathematicians van Ceulen's 35 places. Leibniz's series for a quarter of pi was printed in the Leipzig Acta in 1682. Elsewhere: Leipzig: Acta Eruditorum (since 1682).
- **Trigonometry** [`trigonometry`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/trigonometry.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Tables of sines, tangents and their logarithms are standard for astronomers, surveyors and fortress engineers; a siege engineer computes trench angles with them. Local: fortress engineers (Georg Rimpler, Daniel Suttinger).
- **Coordinate geometry and graphs of functions** [`coordinate_geometry`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/coordinate_geometry.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Descartes's Geometria in van Schooten's Latin edition is known to a few mathematicians. Curves are still mostly treated in the Greek manner; no negative axes, no plotted data. Elsewhere: Leiden: van Schooten's school; Paris.
- **Non-Euclidean geometry** [`non_euclidean_geometry`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/non_euclidean_geometry.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept low
- **Linear perspective and technical drawing** [`perspective_technical_drawing`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/perspective_technical_drawing.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Court theatre sets, fortress plans and bird's-eye city views show full command of perspective. Machines are drawn as pictures, not as dimensioned views a stranger could build from. Local: Lodovico Ottavio Burnacini, court theatre engineer; fortress engineers' plans.
- **Surveying, levelling and triangulation** [`surveying_triangulation`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/surveying_triangulation.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Engineers survey fortress and siege works with plane table, chain and graduated circle. Country maps are compiled from itineraries and sightings, not from a measured triangle net. Local: Georg Matthäus Vischer's map of Lower Austria (1670); Daniel Suttinger, military engineer (Leander Anguissola, in the estates' service at Brünn, comes only in 1684); mine surveyors. Elsewhere: France: Picard's triangulation with telescopic sights.
- **Solar calendar with leap years** [`solar_calendar_leap_years`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/solar_calendar_leap_years.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Vienna uses the Gregorian calendar. Protestant Germany, England and Sweden are ten days behind, so letters from Guericke, Leibniz or London carry old-style or double dates.
- **Decimal, coherent system of units (metric system)** [`metric_system_units`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/metric_system_units.md) — K1, use none, make medium, accept low. Klafter, Schuh, Elle, Eimer, Metzen and Pfund differ from town to town and are not decimal. Changing measures touches tolls and rents; estates and guilds will resist. Elsewhere: Lyon: Mouton's decimal measure from the Earth (1670); London: Wilkins (1668).
- **Probability and statistics** [`probability_statistics`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/probability_statistics.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept medium. Huygens's tract on dice games (1657) is known to few. The city has recorded its dead since 1648, but nobody has counted them as Graunt did in London. Local: Vienna death-inspection registers (Totenbeschauprotokolle); physicians after the plague of 1679. Elsewhere: London: Graunt and Petty; The Hague: Huygens; Hudde and de Witt on annuities.
- **Bayes' theorem (updating belief by evidence)** [`bayes_theorem`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/bayes_theorem.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept low
- **Errors of measurement, the bell curve and least squares** [`normal_distribution_errors`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/normal_distribution_errors.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept medium. Astronomers repeat observations and pick the one they trust or a rough middle. No theory of error; gunners blame every miss on powder or wind.
- **Graphs of data (line, bar and pie charts)** [`data_graphs`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/data_graphs.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept medium. Numbers are shown in tables only. A line of daily deaths, powder stock or flour against the calendar would be new and readable by any officer.
- **Calculus (differentiation and integration)** [`calculus`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/calculus.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept low. Indivisibles and the centre-of-gravity rules of the Jesuit Guldin, who taught in Vienna and Graz, are known. Leibniz prints his differential calculus in October 1684; Newton's is unpublished. Local: Guldin, Centrobaryca (Vienna 1635–1641). Elsewhere: Hanover: Leibniz; Cambridge: Newton; Leipzig: Acta Eruditorum; Kieslingswalde near Görlitz: Tschirnhaus.
- **Infinite series and the number e** [`infinite_series_e`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/infinite_series_e.md) — K1, use none, make hard, accept low. Mercator's logarithm series (1668) and Leibniz's series for pi (1682) are in print for those who get the journals; they are admired as curiosities, not used. Elsewhere: Hanover: Leibniz; Basel: Jakob Bernoulli; Cambridge: Newton's binomial series, unpublished.
